title: Should Rich Countries Cancel Poor Countries’ Debt?
summary: Josh and Chuck examine whether rich countries should cancel poor countries' sovereign debt. They cover the idea of odious debt (Spanish-American War and Cuba, South Africa's apartheid debt), the argument that colonial plunder and post-colonial trade inequality justify debt cancellation as a long overdue payment, the Democratic Republic of Congo under Leopold and Mobutu, the 1970s oil shocks and 1980s debt crisis (Volcker shock, Peru's Alan Garcia, Mexico and Brazil), IMF and World Bank structural adjustment programs, Thomas Sankara's opposition, the Jubilee 2000 campaign led by Bono and Martin Dent, the 2008 Jubilee Act with Spencer Bachus and Maxine Waters, the 2000s HIPC initiative, the post-2008 easy-money borrowing boom, COVID-era debt, the shift to private and Chinese lenders (including Glencore's stake in Chad's debt), G20 payment suspensions, debt-for-nature swaps, climate debt, and a 2022 study on resource extraction from the global South. The episode ends with listener mail: corrections about wolf pack and the Segway inventor, and a story about a father's cremains-paint joke.

segments.title: Opening preamble
segments.summary: Chuck urges listeners to stick with the episode on global debt and debt cancellation, arguing it is fundamental to understanding politics and the global economy.

segments.title: Terminology and framing the global North and South
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck discuss terms for income-level countries (global South, low and middle income, developed and undeveloped) and frame the debate: the global North has exploited the global South, and debt cancellation is argued as a fairness measure.

segments.title: Odious debt and historical examples
segments.summary: They explain odious debt using a stolen credit card analogy, then cover the Spanish-American War debt imposed on Cuba via the Paris Peace Treaty, and South Africa's African National Congress refusing apartheid-era debt, which it later had to repay after the Soviet Union collapsed.

segments.title: Post-colonialism and reparations framing
segments.summary: The hosts argue that European colonial plunder shaped unequal paths for nations, that debt relief can be seen as a long overdue payment for labor rather than charity, and that post-colonial exploitation continued through interventions such as the United Fruit Company's role in Guatemala and through trade inequality.

segments.title: Sponsor break
segments.summary: Brief break before the next segment.

segments.title: Democratic Republic of Congo and the 1970s oil shock
segments.summary: The DRC serves as a through-line example: Leopold's brutal rubber and ivory regime, the 1960 assassination of Patrice Lumumba with Belgian and US support, and Mobutu's looting that drove debt from 5 to 150 percent of GDP. The hosts argue lenders knew and did not care, and that corporations' profit-maximizing behavior needs scrutiny. The 1970s oil price shock then pushed oil exporters to lend to developing countries.

segments.title: Volcker shock and 1980s debt crisis
segments.summary: Oil price inflation in the US and the early 1980s led Paul Volcker to raise interest rates sharply, triggering a global recession. Debtor countries such as Mexico and Brazil could not service their loans, and Peru's Alan Garcia capped debt payments, which led to hyperinflation and loss of investor trust.

segments.title: IMF and World Bank lending and structural adjustment
segments.summary: The IMF and World Bank became multilateral lenders controlled by rich countries, including the Paris Club. Their structural adjustment programs required tax increases, cuts to social spending, privatization, and trade liberalization, with Western advisors sent to help. Critics called these programs neocolonial.

segments.title: Thomas Sankara and resistance to debt
segments.summary: Thomas Sankara, president of Burkina Faso, called in 1987 for African nations not to pay colonial-era debt and was assassinated months later in a coup. The hosts say his death deterred others and that the debt framing he left still influences views today.

segments.title: Jubilee 2000 campaign and the 2008 Jubilee Act
segments.summary: Martin Dent proposed using the millennium as a Jubilee to wipe debts, a idea Bono championed through Jubilee 2000, which helped cancel about 130 billion dollars. Republican Spencer Bachus and Democrat Maxine Waters worked together to pass the Jubilee Act in 2008, and other creditors followed.

segments.title: HIPC initiative and the 2008 financial crisis
segments.summary: Discussion of the Heavily Indebted Poor Countries initiative and how a 70 percent reduction was initially planned for 33 countries. Debt relief worked for much of the 2000s and 2010s. After the 2008 financial crisis, near-zero interest rates made borrowing cheap and countries took on more debt.

segments.title: Easy money analogy and the COVID shock
segments.summary: The hosts compare national borrowing to personal debt and say cheap credit led to over-borrowing, which was exposed when COVID-19 dried up money and raised borrowing needs.

segments.title: Debt burden after COVID-19
segments.summary: Developing nations' debt rose from 2.1 trillion dollars in 2000 to 11.1 trillion in 2021. External debt to gross national income among these countries rose from 17 percent in 2010 to 48.5 percent in 2021. Inflation and rising rates made debt harder to service.

segments.title: Shift to private and Chinese lenders
segments.summary: African external debt is increasingly owed to private creditors at higher rates, and to China, which has filled a void. Private lenders lack strings-attached conditions but charge high interest. Glencore reportedly holds about a third of Chad's national debt, secured against natural resources.

segments.title: G20 suspension and debt restructuring difficulty
segments.summary: The G20 suspended some interest payments during COVID, a temporary measure rather than cancellation. The hosts say the many creditors, including China and private lenders, make coordinated debt cancellation hard, and that taxpayers may end up bailing out private lenders.

segments.title: Debt-for-nature swaps and climate debt
segments.summary: Debt-for-nature deals, such as the Nature Conservancy arrangement in Belize in 2021, cancel debt in exchange for conservation spending. The hosts argue that climate change harms poorer countries that contributed little, and that climate-vulnerable nations face higher borrowing costs.

segments.title: Quantifying colonial labor and resource extraction
segments.summary: Historian Hilary Beckles estimated about 8 trillion dollars of free labor in the Caribbean over two centuries. A 2022 study by academics found that in 2015 the global North appropriated about 12 billion tons of raw materials, 822 million hectares of land and 392 billion hours of labor, valued at 10.8 trillion dollars.

segments.title: Closing argument and caution to listeners
segments.summary: Chuck says listeners who disagree are fine as long as they research the complexity of world economies, and makes a brief joke about Karens and Chads.

segments.title: Listener mail: corrections and a cremains paint joke
segments.summary: Corrections: wolf pack is a regional term, and the Segway company owner Jimmy Heselden, not the inventor, rode off a cliff. A recommended Cautionary Tales episode is mentioned. A listener, Zach Mitchell of Saint Louis, shares how his father's cremated ashes were mixed into paint for his mother's bedroom ceiling as a longtime joke.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts thank listeners and invite email; the show credits iHeartRadio.
